content: 1. The Rome Declaration on Nutrition was an outcome document from the Second International Conference on Nutrition held in Rome from November 19 to 21, 2014. This document outlines global commitments to addressing malnutrition in all its forms and emphasizes the importance of sustainable food systems in promoting health and nutrition. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides a comprehensive resource on the double burden of malnutrition, which refers to the coexistence of undernutrition and overweight/obesity within individuals, households, and populations. This resource is accessible on the WHO website and was last accessed on November 4, 2016. 3. Grijalva-Eternod et al. conducted a cross-sectional study on Western Sahara refugees, highlighting the double burden of obesity and malnutrition in a protracted emergency setting. The findings, published in PLoS Medicine in 2012, underscore the complex interplay of nutritional challenges in such populations. 4. The Global Strategy for Infant and Young Child Feeding, developed by WHO and UNICEF, provides evidence-based recommendations to improve feeding practices and nutritional outcomes for children. This document was accessed on November 4, 2016. 5. The Lancet Breastfeeding Series Group published a comprehensive analysis in 2016 on breastfeeding in the 21st century, detailing its epidemiology, biological mechanisms, and lifelong health effects. The study emphasizes the critical role of breastfeeding in reducing morbidity and mortality. 6. WHO and UNICEF developed the Model IMCI Handbook, which serves as a guide for the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI). This resource provides practical tools for healthcare workers to address common childhood illnesses and was accessed on January 20, 2017. 7. The Integrated Management of Childhood Illness Chart Booklet is a concise reference for healthcare providers, offering algorithms and guidelines for managing childhood illnesses. This document was accessed on January 20, 2017. 8. WHO and UNICEF also created a course on infant and young child feeding counseling, integrating nutrition education into healthcare practices. This course material was accessed on November 4, 2016. 9. The Essential Newborn Care Course, published by WHO in 2010, provides training for healthcare workers on evidence-based practices to improve neonatal outcomes. This resource was accessed on November 5, 2016. 10. WHO developed a training course for community health workers on caring for newborns and children in the community, focusing on home-based care for newborns. This material was accessed on November 5, 2016. 11. Another WHO training course for community health workers addresses the care of sick children, emphasizing the management of common childhood illnesses. This resource was accessed on November 5, 2016. 12. WHO also offers a training course on promoting healthy growth and development in children, targeting community health workers. This document was accessed on November 5, 2016. 13. The Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s, and Adolescents’ Health (2016–2030) outlines a framework for improving health outcomes through survival, thriving, and transformation. This strategy was accessed on November 5, 2016. 14. WHO’s guidelines on managing severe acute malnutrition in infants and children provide evidence-based recommendations for healthcare providers. This document was accessed on November 4, 2016. 15. The WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children, second edition, offers guidelines for managing common childhood illnesses in hospital settings. This resource was accessed on November 4, 2016. 16. McDonald et al. conducted a meta-analysis of 10 prospective studies from developing countries, examining the impact of multiple anthropometric deficits on child mortality. The findings, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2013, highlight the critical role of addressing growth deficits in reducing mortality. 17. The Essential Nutrition Actions framework focuses on improving maternal, newborn, infant, and young child nutrition through evidence-based interventions. This document was accessed on November 4, 2016. 18. Barros and Victora conducted a meta-analysis of epidemiological data from 63 lowand middle-income countries, examining the prevalence of underweight, wasting, and stunting in children. This analysis provides regional insights into malnutrition trends. 19. Singh et al. systematically reviewed the relationship between anthropometric measures during infancy and childhood and the risk of developing obesity, cardiovascular disease, or type 2 diabetes later in life. This review highlights the long-term health implications of early growth patterns. 20. Flandez surveyed IMCI chart booklets and clinical algorithms used in various countries, reporting on the uptake and adaptations of IMCI at the national level. This survey provides insights into the implementation of IMCI guidelines. 21. Grobler et al. reviewed the benefits and harms of supplementary foods for moderately and severely undernourished infants and children aged 6–59 months. This review evaluates the effectiveness of nutritional interventions in improving health outcomes. 22. Systematic reviews of interventions to prevent or treat obesity in children were conducted using a structured process, including search strategies, screening, and grading of evidence. These reviews address key questions in population, intervention, comparison, and outcome (PICO) format. 23. The WHO Global Strategy on Diet, Physical Activity, and Health provides recommendations for promoting healthy lifestyles and preventing non-communicable diseases. This strategy emphasizes the importance of physical activity and balanced nutrition. 24. The WHO e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions (eLENA) is an online resource providing evidence-based guidance on nutrition interventions. This library was accessed on November 8, 2016. 25. A combined course on growth assessment and infant and young child feeding, developed by WHO, integrates nutritional assessment into healthcare practices. This course material was accessed on November 4, 2012. 26. Gaye and Steele conducted a meta-analysis of motivational interviewing interventions for pediatric health behavior change, demonstrating their effectiveness in promoting healthier behaviors in children. 27. Wang et al. systematically reviewed childhood obesity prevention programs, identifying effective strategies and interventions. This review provides evidence-based recommendations for reducing obesity prevalence in children. 28. Redsell et al. reviewed randomized controlled trials of interventions aimed at reducing the risk of overweight and obesity in infancy and early childhood. This review highlights the importance of early prevention efforts. 29. Laws et al. examined the impact of interventions to prevent obesity or improve obesity-related behaviors in children from socioeconomically disadvantaged or indigenous families. This review emphasizes the need for targeted approaches in vulnerable populations. 30. Dobbins et al. reviewed school-based physical activity programs for promoting physical activity and fitness in children and adolescents aged 6–18 years. This review highlights the role of schools in fostering healthy behaviors. 31. Hearnshaw and Matyka discussed the management of childhood obesity, emphasizing the need for additional interventions when lifestyle changes alone are insufficient. This review explores alternative strategies for addressing obesity in children.
